common_name: Beverley Brook Boston Ivy (Compact Small-Leaf Japanese Creeper)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade near a wall or fence for the self-clinging tendrils to grip; this selection suits smaller properties better than the vigorous wild species.

directions: Beverley Brook arose as a chance seedling found growing beside a London roadway before the Second World War and was selected for its noticeably restrained vigor compared with ordinary Boston ivy. Its three-lobed leaves run smaller than the species, giving a finer-textured, denser cover on walls, fences, and tree trunks that the adhesive tendril discs grip without extra support. Autumn still brings the same reliable shift into brilliant scarlet before leaf drop, but the slower overall growth makes this form easier to keep within bounds on garden walls or compact spaces. Site it in partial shade to full sun and prune lightly in late winter if growth needs tidying near windows or trim.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Green Spring Boston Ivy (Large-Leaf Japanese Creeper)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; give it generous space since its leaves and overall habit run larger than most Boston ivy selections.

directions: Green Spring was raised in France and named in the mid-1960s for its notably oversized leaves, often spanning six to ten inches across, far larger than the typical three-lobed foliage of wild Boston ivy. The glossy, deep green summer leaves shift to a rich reddish-purple before falling, giving a bolder, more dramatic seasonal display than smaller-leaved selections. Like the species it self-clings with adhesive tendril discs and needs no trellis or wire support once established on masonry, wood, or a sturdy trunk. Because of its large leaf size and vigor, give it generous wall space and prune back growth that strays toward windows, gutters, or rooflines.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Ginza Lights Boston Ivy (Pink-and-White Variegated Japanese Creeper)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; the pink-tinted new growth colors best out of harsh afternoon sun.

directions: Ginza Lights produces smaller leaves than the species that emerge in soft shades of pink and white before settling into green for summer, giving spring growth an unusually soft, pastel look among Boston ivy selections. By autumn the foliage shifts again, turning a vivid crimson that rivals the species for fall color even though the plant stays comparatively compact and refined. It climbs by the same self-clinging adhesive discs as other Parthenocissus tricuspidata forms, gripping masonry, wood, or stone without wires or trellising. Grow in partial shade for the best color contrast in the pink-and-white new growth, and prune in late winter to keep it off windows and gutters.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Skylands Giant Climbing Hydrangea (Large-Flowered Climbing Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall, fence, or sturdy tree trunk the vine can self-cling to; allow extra wall space for its eventually large size.

directions: Skylands Giant was selected before 2000 at the New Jersey State Botanical Garden at Skylands and is grown chiefly for its oversized flattened lacecap flower clusters, which can reach roughly a foot across, well beyond the size typical of the species. Its glossy green summer foliage turns a clear yellow in autumn, adding a second season of interest after the early-summer bloom fades. Like other climbing hydrangea forms it clings to brick, stone, or wood with aerial rootlets and needs no trellis, though it grows slowly for its first few seasons while establishing roots. Site it in partial shade in moist, humus-rich soil and give it a sturdy, large wall or trunk, since the oversized blooms come from an eventually substantial vine.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Sutter's Mill Climbing Hydrangea (Gold-Leaved Climbing Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall, fence, or sturdy tree trunk the vine can self-cling to.

directions: Sutter's Mill, named for the California gold rush site, opens with bright yellow spring foliage that gradually mellows to a lighter green as the leaves mature through summer. The color progression gives the vine a changeable look through the season, useful for brightening a shaded wall or fence before settling into a calmer green backdrop for the white lacecap flower clusters. It self-clings with aerial rootlets the way other climbing hydrangea selections do, requiring no trellis once it has gripped brick, stone, or wood. Give it partial shade and shelter from hot afternoon sun, which can scorch the yellow new growth, and be patient through the first few slow-to-establish seasons.

common_name: Jeanne Barret Climbing Hydrangea (Compact Dwarf Climbing Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall, fence, or sturdy tree trunk the vine can self-cling to; its smaller ultimate size fits tighter spaces than standard climbing hydrangea.

directions: Jeanne Barret traces to a wild collection made on Kyushu, Japan, and was later named and promoted in France in 2013 in honor of the eighteenth-century botanist-explorer of the same name. It grows distinctly less vigorously than the species, making it a better fit for smaller gardens or more contained wall spaces where a full-sized climbing hydrangea would quickly outgrow its spot. Like other forms it clings by aerial rootlets to brick, stone, or wood and produces the same flattened white lacecap flower clusters in early summer once established. Plant in partial shade in moist, well-drained soil and expect a slower, more restrained spread than standard climbing hydrangea.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
